div.head: Wi Prolog., Prol. 1, Prol. 2, Prol. 3
div.ab: Ðam mildestan cyninge Cantwara Wihtræde rixigendum þe fiftan wintra his rices, þy niguðan gebanne, sextan dæge Rugernes, in þære stowe þy hatte Berghamstyde, ðær wæs gesamnad eadigra geheahtendlic ymcyme: ðær wæs Birhtwald, Bretone heahbiscop, ⁊ se ær næmda cyning; eac þan Hrofesceastre bisceop (se ilca Gybmund wæs haten) andward wæs; ⁊ cwæð ælc had ciricean ðære mægðe anmodlice mid þy hersuman folcy. Þær ða eadigan fundon mid ealra gemedum ðas domas ⁊ Cantwara rihtum þeawum æcton, swa hit hyr efter segeþ ⁊ cwyþ:

Ðam mildestan cyninge Cantwara Wihtræde rixigendum þe fiftan wintra his rices, þy niguðan gebanne, sextan dæge Rugernes, in þære stowe þy hatte Berghamstyde, ðær wæs gesamnad eadigra geþeahtendlic ymcyme. Ðær wæs Birhtwald, Bretone heahbiscop, ⁊ se ær næmda cyning; eac þan Hrofesceastre bisceop (se ilca Gybmund wæs haten) andward wæs; ⁊ cwæð ælc had ciricean ðære mægðe anmodlice mid þy hersuman folcy. Ðær ða eadigan fundon mid ealra gemedum ðas domas ⁊ Cantwara rihtum þeawum æcton, swa hit hyr efter segeþ ⁊ cwyþ:

Ðam mildestan cyninge Cantwara Wihtrede, rixigendum þe fiftan wintra his rices, þy niguðan gebanne, sextan dæge Rugernes, in þære stowe þy hatte Berghamstyde, ðær wæs gesamnad eadigra ge[þ]eahtendlic ymcyme: Ðær wæs Birhtwald Bretone heahbiscop, ⁊ se ærnæmda cyning; eac þan Hrofesceastre bisceop, se ilca Gybmund wæs haten, andward wæs; ⁊ cwæð ælc had ciricean ðære mægðe anmodlice mid þy hersuman folcy. Þær ða eadigan fundon mid ealra gemedum ðas domas ⁊ Cantwara rihtum þeawum æcton, swa hit hyr efter segeþ ⁊ cwyþ:

Als der gnädigste König der Kenter Wihtred herrschte im fünften Jahre seiner Regirung, in der neunten Indiction, am sechsten Tage des [Monats] Rugern, da war an dem Orte, der Berstead heisst, berathende Versammlung der Grossen versammelt: [Prol., 1] da war Birhtwald, Britanniens Erzbischof, und der vorher genannte König; nächstdem war Rochesters Bischof (derselbe war Gybmund geheissen) gegenwärtig; [Prol., 2] und es sprach jeder Grad der Kirche dieser Nation einmüthig mit dem gehorsamen [Laien]volke. [Prol., 3] Da bestimmten die Grossen mit Zustimmung Aller und fügten zu den rechtsgültigen Bräuchen der Kenter folgende Gesetze, wie es hier nachstehend lautet und heisst:

When the most gracious king of the Kentish people, Wihtred, was reigning in the fifth year of his reign, in the ninth indiction, on the sixth day of [the month of] Rugern, there was assembled at the place called Bearsted a deliberative assembly of the great men: [Prol., 1] there was Birhtwald, archbishop of Britain, and the king named before; next, the bishop of Rochester (the same was called Gybmund) was present; [Prol., 2] and every rank of the Church of this nation spoke with one mind together with the obedient [lay] people. [Prol., 3] Then the great men, with the consent of all, determined and added to the lawful customs of the Kentish people the following laws, as it reads and says hereafter:

During the sovereignty of Wihtred, the most gracious king of Kent, in the fifth year of his reign, the ninth Indiction, the sixth day of Rugern, in a place which is called Barham, there was assembled a deliberative council of the notables. There were present there Berhtwald, the chief bishop of Britain, and the above-mentioned king; the bishop of Rochester, who was called Gefmund; and every order of the Church of the province expressed itself in unanimity with the loyal laity [assembled there]. There the notables, with the consent of all, drew up these decrees, and added them to the legal usages of the people of Kent, as is hereafter stated and declared:

When the most gracious king of the people of Kent, Wihtred, was reigning, in the fifth year of his reign, the ninth indiction, on the sixth day of Rugern, in the place which is called Berghamstyde, there was collected a deliberative assembly of leading men. Brihtwold, archbishop of Britain, was there, and the above-named king; also the bishop of Rochester, who was called Gefmund, was present; and every order of the Church of that nation spoke in unanimity with the loyal people. There, with the consent of all, the leading men devised these decrees and added them to the lawful usages of the people of Kent, as it says and declares hereafter.

To the most gracious king of the Kentish people, Wihtred, ruling in the fifth winter of his reign, in the ninth indiction, sixth day of Rugern, in that place which is called Berghamstead, there was gathered a consilary assembly of great men. There was Brihtwald, archbishop of Britain, and the afore-mentioned king; likewise the bishop of Rochester, which same was called Gebmund, was present; and each order of the church of that people spoke with a single mind with the loyal populace. There the great men devised, with the consent of all, these decrees, and added to the just customs of the Kentish people, as it hereafter says and declares:

note.label: same idiom (ecan, 'to supplement')
note.quote: Alfred makes use of an idiom earlier employed by Hloðhere and Eadric, Wihtred, and Ine in the prologues to their respective codes

note.label: same distinction (æw/domas)
note.quote: This doublet maintains the distinction between æw [...] and domas [...] found also in the prologues to the Kentish laws of Hloþhere and Eadric and Wihtred | Ine's self-assertion in his brief prologue is in marked contrast to Wihtred's presence at the outset of his laws

note.seg: bessere geþeahtendlic
read geþeahtendlic
Dativus absolutus; s. d. Wb 46; Mätzner Engl. Gram. II 2, 73. Zur erzählenden Form s. Hl Pro²
Dativus absolutus; see that word in Wb 46; Mätzner Engl. Gram. II 2, 73. On the narrative form see Hl Pro²
milde heisst hier ‘serenus, propitius’, wie im 10. Jh. hold; s. Wb. Auch der Freibrief von Bapchild beginnt praesidente Wihtredo clementissimo rege Cantuariorum; Bi 91
milde here means ‘serenus, propitius’, like hold in the 10th cent.; see Wb. The charter of privilege of Bapchild likewise begins praesidente Wihtredo clementissimo rege Cantuariorum; Bi 91
‘Winter’ passt nicht, wenn Rugern ein Erntemonat ist. Es steht für ‘Jahr’; s. d. Gl 1
‘Winter’ does not fit if Rugern is a harvest month. It stands for ‘year’; see that word in Gl 1

Da der Name Indiktion (s. d. Gl) richtig durch Bridferht von Ramsey (zu Bedas Temp. rat. 48) von indicere, inde imperiale præceptum hergeleitet wird, so nennen sie die Agsa. ‘Befehl’. Später findet sich dafür a. 860 tacncircul: ‘Periode von Jahren’

Since the name Indiction (see that word in Gl) is correctly derived by Bridferht of Ramsey (on Beda’s Temp. rat. 48) from indicere, inde imperiale præceptum, the Anglo-Saxons call it ‘command’. Later, a. 860, tacncircul is found for it: ‘period of years’

Im Ggs. zum Lateinischen, von künftigen Kal., Non., Id. datierenden, Kalender zählen die Tage nách Monatsbeginn in Urkk. auch Erzb. Theodor 24. Sept. 673, K. Ceadwalla 3. Aug. 683, Erzb. Berhtwald 30. Juli 683, K. Swæbred 13. Juni 704

In contrast to the Latin calendar, which dates from the coming Kal., Non., Id., the days are counted from the beginning of the month in charters also by Archbp. Theodore 24 Sept. 673, King Ceadwalla 3 Aug. 683, Archbp. Berhtwald 30 July 683, King Swæbred 13 June 704

Rugern (o. S. 24 n. 8) deutete Grimm ‘Roggenernte’ 1841 Kl. Schri. V 321; die Deutung ruhgeorn liess er Gesch. Dt. Spra. 81 fort. [Er dachte beim Gäl. rioghail an Rugern; jenes hielt er aber nur irrig für ‘August’, es bedeutet augustus ‘erhaben’; Zimmer 1896 brieflich.] Der Litauer benennt den August nach dem Roggen, der Mecklenburger eine Sommerzeit roggaust; Weinhold Monatsnamen 53. Viele Monatsnamen sind gebildet von einer Pflanze als erstem Gliede, andere mit ‘Schnitt(Ernte)’ als zweitem Gliede, vgl. barleymonth, -sele, bonenarne, beansele ‘time of beanharvest’; 17 Beispiele bei Weinhold; Schrader 550

Grimm interpreted Rugern (above p. 24 n. 8) as ‘rye harvest’ in 1841, Kl. Schri. V 321; in Gesch. Dt. Spra. 81 he dropped the interpretation ruhgeorn. [He connected Gaelic rioghail with Rugern; but he merely mistook the former for ‘August’; it means augustus ‘exalted’; Zimmer, by letter, 1896.] The Lithuanians name August after rye, the people of Mecklenburg call a summer season roggaust; Weinhold Monatsnamen 53. Many month-names are formed with a plant as first element, others with ‘cutting (harvest)’ as second element, cf. barleymonth, -sele, bonenarne, beansele ‘time of beanharvest’; 17 examples in Weinhold; Schrader 550
Gegen die Übersetzung ‘where’ spricht die Wortstellung
The word order tells against the translation ‘where’

‘Berkhampstead’, an das die Erklärer vor Price dachten, scheint zu weit nordwestlich von Kent entfernt (obwohl, da im 12. Jh. von Königen bewohnt und an der Strasse, es geeignet lag für eine Versammlung ganz Südenglands, wie das nur 6 Meilen westliche Hertford 673). Es lag in Mercien, während hier ein rein Kentisches Gemot gemeint ist. — ‘Barham’, 1¹/₂ Meilen südlich von Canterbury, auf das Price (auch Chadwick Ags. instit. 252) riet, heisst schon im Domesday Berham. Allerdings ist -stede auch hinter zwei anderen Ortsnamen auf -ham (bei Chichester in der Urk. a. 714) abgefallen, wenn die Identifikation bei Birch n. 132 richtig ist. Kemble erklärt ‘Berste(a)d’, ³/₄ Meile östlich Maidstone (Saxons II 207. 244; danach Stubbs Councils III 238, Parker Early Oxford 192; Pearman Rochester 33. Plummer Saxon chron. II p. x identifiziert damit Beorhhamsted der Ann. Agsax. a. 1066 D. Eine andere Form o. Sp. 1, Z. 2). Dieses Kirchspiel hiess um 1100 und noch um 1367 Berghestede und enthält ein Landgut Moathall, das vielleicht nach einstigem gemot heisst; Hasted Hist. of Kent II 486. 489; Catal. anc. deeds I C 1016. Dieselbe Abschleifung des Namens zeigt das Beorganstede, Berghestede jetzt Berstead, bei Chichester (Bi 50; Sussex archl. coll. 24, 166; Ellis and Bickley Index to the charters in the Brit. Mus. I 66) und in Kent Perhamstede, das im 12. Jh. Perstede lautet (irrig mit Berstead identifiziert; Stubbs Councils III 238 aus Bi 176 [wozu Kemble VI 321 ‘Berstead’ erklärt], einem Auszuge aus Bi 199; diese Örtlichkeit erhellt aus Bi 247f. 263)

‘Berkhampstead’, which commentators before Price had in mind, seems too far north-west of Kent (although, as it was inhabited by kings in the 12th cent. and lay on the highroad, it was well situated for an assembly of all southern England, like Hertford, only 6 miles to the west, in 673). It lay in Mercia, whereas a purely Kentish gemot is meant here. — ‘Barham’, 1¹/₂ miles south of Canterbury, which Price (also Chadwick Ags. instit. 252) guessed at, is already called Berham in Domesday. Admittedly, -stede has also dropped off after two other place-names in -ham (near Chichester, in the charter a. 714), if the identification in Birch n. 132 is correct. Kemble explains it as ‘Berste(a)d’, ³/₄ mile east of Maidstone (Saxons II 207. 244; following him Stubbs Councils III 238, Parker Early Oxford 192; Pearman Rochester 33. Plummer Saxon chron. II p. x identifies with it the Beorhhamsted of the Ann. Agsax. a. 1066 D. Another form above col. 1, l. 2). This parish was called Berghestede about 1100 and still about 1367, and contains an estate Moathall, which is perhaps named after a former gemot; Hasted Hist. of Kent II 486. 489; Catal. anc. deeds I C 1016. The same wearing-down of the name is shown by Beorganstede, Berghestede, now Berstead, near Chichester (Bi 50; Sussex archl. coll. 24, 166; Ellis and Bickley Index to the charters in the Brit. Mus. I 66) and, in Kent, by Perhamstede, which in the 12th cent. appears as Perstede (wrongly identified with Berstead; Stubbs Councils III 238 from Bi 176 [which Kemble VI 321 explains as ‘Berstead’], an extract from Bi 199; this locality is made clear by Bi 247f. 263)

Die Verbindung eines *geheahtendlic mit heah durch Lye ist unglücklich. Price’s Emendation des Schreibfehlers (s. Wb 216 Sp. 2 n. 10; 107 Sp. 3 n. 4e) wird gestützt durch das geþeaht (s. Wb) in genau demselben Zusammenhang bei Beginn von Gesetzen und Urkk.: mid minra witena geþeahte a. 1061 Ke 1341; mid geþeahtunge Ælfreds Testament (Bi 553). Vgl. auch geþeahtend, -ta, -tere ‘consiliarius’, geþeahtian ‘consiliari’, ungeþeahtendlic ‘inconsiderate’

Lye’s connection of a *geheahtendlic with heah is infelicitous. Price’s emendation of the scribal error (see Wb 216 col. 2 n. 10; 107 col. 3 n. 4e) is supported by geþeaht (see Wb) in exactly the same context at the beginning of laws and charters: mid minra witena geþeahte a. 1061 Ke 1341; mid geþeahtunge Ælfred’s will (Bi 553). Cf. also geþeahtend, -ta, -tere ‘consiliarius’, geþeahtian ‘consiliari’, ungeþeahtendlic ‘inconsiderate’
eadig ‘vornehm, mächtig’, übertragen von ‘reich, glücklich’, wie rice, dives (s. d. Wb) und in Spanien Ricos hombres; Kemble Saxons II 199
eadig ‘noble, powerful’, transferred from ‘rich, fortunate’, like rice, dives (see that word in Wb) and in Spain Ricos hombres; Kemble Saxons II 199

Erwählt 1. Juli 692, geweiht 29. Juni 693, † 13. Jan. 731; Beda V 8. 23; Ann. Anglosax. Er war als Abt von Reculver vom Kenterkönig Hlothaere 679 beschenkt worden; Bi 45; vgl. Stubbs Councils III 228. Nicht identisch ist er mit dem Abt von Glastenbury; Plummer Bede II 283

Elected 1 July 692, consecrated 29 June 693, † 13 Jan. 731; Beda V 8. 23; Ann. Anglosax. As abbot of Reculver he had received a grant from Hlothaere, king of Kent, in 679; Bi 45; cf. Stubbs Councils III 228. He is not identical with the abbot of Glastonbury; Plummer Bede II 283
Nicht ‘der Briten’. Theodor nennt sich 680 archiepiscopus Brittaniae. Und Berctvaldo totius Brettaniae gubernacula regenti schreibt der Bischof von London a. 705 Bi 115
Not ‘of the Britons’. Theodore calls himself archiepiscopus Brittaniae in 680. And the bishop of London writes Berctvaldo totius Brettaniae gubernacula regenti a. 705, Bi 115
heahbisceop für das gewöhnlichere ærceb- auch sonst; s. Wb und Toller. Vgl. Gl Erzbischof 6; u. 16²
heahbisceop for the more usual ærceb- occurs elsewhere too; see Wb and Toller. Cf. Gl Erzbischof 6; below 16²
Nicht ‘auch dann’; eac regiert den folgenden Kasus þan (‘hinzu, ausser- (nebst)dem’) und bildet damit Einen Begriff; so bietet eacþon: quinetiam, ceterum Toller Suppl.
Not ‘also then’; eac governs the following case þan (‘in addition, besides (together with) that’) and forms a single concept with it; thus Toller Suppl. gives eacþon: quinetiam, ceterum

Gebmund ward einige Zeit nach 676 von Theodor, der 690 starb, geweiht; Beda IV 12. Er starb längere Zeit vor 706 (da wird Bi 116 bezeugt vom Nachfolger Tobias), aber nicht schon 693, zu welchem Annale der Agsä. Annalist den Tod ausdrücklich nur ungefähr ansetzt, veranlasst von Beda, der zur Inthronisation Berhtwalds auch dessen Bischofsweihen meldete, darunter die von Gebmunds Nachfolger. [Flor. Wig. folgt ebenfalls Beda; erst die Kompilation von St. Albans vom Anfang 13. Jhs. verschuldet durch Fortlassung des Zwischensatzes den Fehler, diese Weihe 693 anzusetzen.] Der Nachfolger wohnt zwar der Synode von Bapchild bei; diese ist aber 694 nur ‘ungefähr’ eingeordnet und hat kein echtes Datum überliefert; Stubbs Councils III 232. 241. Gebmund erscheint in einer Urk. von 693 und dreien von 696. 699, die aber unecht sind; Bi 85. 89f. 99

Gebmund was consecrated some time after 676 by Theodore, who died in 690; Beda IV 12. He died a considerable time before 706 (when Bi 116 is attested by his successor Tobias), but not as early as 693, under which annal the Anglo-Saxon annalist expressly places his death only approximately, prompted by Beda, who, in connection with Berhtwald’s enthronement, also reported the consecrations of bishops performed by him, among them that of Gebmund’s successor. [Flor. Wig. likewise follows Beda; only the St Albans compilation of the beginning of the 13th cent., by omitting the intervening clause, is to blame for the error of placing this consecration in 693.] The successor does indeed attend the synod of Bapchild; but this is placed in 694 only ‘approximately’ and has no genuine date handed down; Stubbs Councils III 232. 241. Gebmund appears in a charter of 693 and in three of 696. 699, which, however, are spurious; Bi 85. 89f. 99
mægð kann zwar neben ‘Volksstamm’ auch ‘Land(esteil)’ bedeuten, wie Frühere übersetzen. Damals aber pflegt sich Volk oder Regent noch nicht nach dem Territorium zu nennen
mægð can indeed mean ‘land (region)’ as well as ‘tribe’, as earlier translators render it. At that time, however, a people or ruler did not yet usually name itself after the territory
folcy ist alter Instrumental. Im Ggs. zum Klerus müssen Laien gemeint sein; s. folcesman u. 24. Vgl. Gl Witan 7. f. 8
folcy is an old instrumental. In contrast to the clergy, laymen must be meant; see folcesman below 24. Cf. Gl Witan 7. f. 8

bei dieser Hs. nicht e(a)cton mit Grimm Kl. Schr. V 321 zu bessern; s. Wb æ-5. — Richtig verstanden iecan schon Wilkins und Price hier anders als in Hl (Schmid und Grimm fallen auf ‘vermehren’ zurück, den Dativ þeawum als Instr. erklärend); es übersetzt auch adiicere Lucas III 20. XII 25 (Toller s. v., auch geiecean) und apponere; z. B. oðrum geiecean þæt (Ælfred’s Gregor ed. Sweet 291²⁵) und ætecte his gehatum (Bede III 27), ætycte his benum V 5; Toller. Das neu Hinzutretende sind domas, das Fortbestehende die Kenter Gewohnheiten; s. Hl Pro, an den diese Worte anklingen; Gl altes Recht 2

in this MS not to be emended to e(a)cton with Grimm Kl. Schr. V 321; see Wb æ-5. — Wilkins and Price already rightly understood iecan here differently from in Hl (Schmid and Grimm fall back on ‘increase’, explaining the dative þeawum as instr.); it also translates adiicere Lucas III 20. XII 25 (Toller s. v., also geiecean) and apponere; e.g. oðrum geiecean þæt (Ælfred’s Gregor ed. Sweet 291²⁵) and ætecte his gehatum (Bede III 27), ætycte his benum V 5; Toller. What is newly added are the domas, what continues in force are the Kentish customs; see Hl Pro, which these words echo; Gl altes Recht 2

note.label: geþeahtendlic
note.seg: em. Thorpe. geheahtendlic. H.
Cf. Plummer, Baedae Opera Historica, ii. p. 38 f.
i.e. perhaps, the month of the rye harvest (August?).
Berghamstyde has been variously identified with Berkhampstead, Barham (near Canterbury), and Berstead (near Maidstone). See Liebermann’s note ad loc.; Chadwick, Anglo-Saxon Institutions, p. 252.

note.label: Rugern
note.seg: Probably September. The word means “rye-harvest”.

note.label: Berghamstyde
note.seg: Birch, No. 88, dated 696, is also issued at this place. Bearsted, near Maidstone, may be meant, for it is derived from the same name, whereas Barham, Kent, which has been suggested, is an earlier Bioraham.

note.label: Britain
note.seg: York did not become an archbishopric until 735.

note.label: ge[þ]eahtendlic
note.seg: Emendation following Liebermann and Bosworth: manuscript reads geheahtendlic.

note.label: reign,
note.seg: Germanic peoples (not surprisingly, given the climate) counted years in winters.

note.label: indiction,
note.seg: The term ‘indiction’ dates back to imperial Rome, when tax assessment was calculated in fifteen-year cycles with the internal years reckoned as indictio primo, secundo, etc. Probably 695: see Commentary under ‘Rubric and prologue’ for further discussion.

note.label: Rugern,
note.seg: Rugern means ‘rye-harvest’: this was probably in September.

note.label: Berghamstead,
note.seg: Perhaps Bearsted, near Maidstone.
